The best sign in my neighborhood was taped to the window of a watch repair shop: BACK IN TEN MINUTES. There was no indication of when the ten minutes had begun. Behind the glass, seventeen clocks offered seventeen opinions about the matter.

I waited. I had brought in my father’s watch, which had started losing about four minutes a day. At first this hadn’t bothered me. Then I missed a train by just enough time to see a woman in a blue coat settle into the window seat I would have chosen.

The watchmaker came back carrying two coffees. He set one on the counter in front of me.

“How did you know somebody would be waiting?”

“I didn’t,” he said. “That one’s for later.”

He opened the watch and bent over it. I drank nothing. From the back room came a single, extravagant cuckoo, though it was twenty past eleven by my phone.

“My dad used to set it five minutes fast,” I said.

“Want me to do that?”

I almost said yes. Then I remembered my father in the hall, patting his pockets for his keys, calling to my mother that they had plenty of time because his watch was five minutes fast. She had already been sitting in the car for ten.

“No,” I said. “Just make it right.”

When I came back on Friday, the watch was ready. The watchmaker set it to the second and buckled it around my wrist. I caught my train with time to spare. The window seat was taken, but the one across from it was free, and it turned out there was a river on that side.
